contractile-cardiomyocyte.def: A working muscle cell of the heart wall (a cardiomyocyte): short, branched and striated, with one or two central nuclei, many mitochondria, and intercalated discs whose gap junctions pass action potentials to its neighbors. It rests at about −90 mV and fires only when charge from a neighbor brings it to threshold.

l-type-calcium.def: Voltage-gated calcium channels in the sarcolemma and T tubules of cardiac muscle cells that open slowly on depolarization and stay open a long time. The calcium entering through them holds the plateau and triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

cardiac-ap.def: The action potential of a contractile ventricular cell, lasting about 250 to 300 ms: a fast sodium upstroke (phase 0), a small notch (phase 1), a plateau near 0 mV where calcium entry balances potassium exit (phase 2), repolarization by potassium exit (phase 3), and rest at about −90 mV (phase 4).

cicr.def: Calcium-induced calcium release: calcium entering a cardiac muscle cell through L-type channels opens calcium release channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases a much larger amount of calcium into the cytosol and starts contraction.

cardiac-refractory.def: In cardiac muscle the absolute refractory period lasts about 200 to 250 ms, because the sodium channels stay inactivated through the plateau. It lasts nearly as long as the contraction, so a new action potential cannot start until the cell is relaxing, and twitches cannot sum into tetanus.
